extracted.intended_audience: general readers, theatre students, researchers and fans of Noël Coward
extracted.subtask_description: An encyclopaedic biographical article summarising Noël Coward's life, career, works, public image and critical reception, including statements of his own views about theatre and performance practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primary purpose of a play — entertain
rubrics_metrics.description: Coward argued that the primary purpose of a play was to entertain, and he made no attempt at modernism, which he felt was boring to the audience although fascinating to the critics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefers entertainment value over avant-garde/modernist experimentation; writing should engage and delight audiences rather than aim primarily to impress critics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid political propaganda in theatre
rubrics_metrics.description: "The theatre must be treated with respect. ... What it most emphatically is not and never will be is a scruffy, ill-lit drill hall serving as a temporary soap-box for political propaganda."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coward's stance: plays should not serve as mere vehicles for political messaging; political material must be integrated respectfully and not reduce the theatre to propaganda.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rely on character interplay rather than elaborate comic machinery
rubrics_metrics.description: Plays like Hay Fever 'depend purely on the interplay of characters, not on elaborate comic machinery.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasises character-driven comedy and interaction over complex plotting or gimmicks; comic effect should arise from relationships and dialogue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid excessive 'smartness' in writing
rubrics_metrics.description: Contemporary critics warned Coward to 'overcome a tendency to smartness' in order to produce more interesting plays.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wittiness should not tip into brittle or superficial 'smartness' that undermines deeper dramatic interest; balance polish with substance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manage length of star engagements (limit long runs)
rubrics_metrics.description: Coward disliked long runs, and after Private Lives he 'made a rule of starring in a play for no more than three months at any venue.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Performance career strategy: limit long residencies to avoid over-exposure and preserve freshness of performances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultivate personal image but avoid overdoing flamboyance
rubrics_metrics.description: Coward 'assiduous[ly] cultivation of a carefully crafted image' but advised friends (e.g., Cecil Beaton) to 'tone down his outfits' because 'It is important not to let the public have a loophole to lampoon you.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deliberate personal branding and style can enhance a public career, but excessive affectation invites ridicule; moderation and control are recommended.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stage risqué material where censorship permits
rubrics_metrics.description: Design for Living was 'so risqué ... that Coward premiered it in New York, knowing that it would not survive the censor in London.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When material is likely to face censorship, choose venues/jurisdictions with more permissive standards to preserve the work's integrity and intended effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protect private life from over-publicity
rubrics_metrics.description: Coward believed his private business was not for public discussion, considering 'any sexual activities when over-advertised' to be tasteless.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain discretion about personal matters; excessive publicising of private life is judged to be in poor taste and can harm professional image.
